Review Outlines Biology-Driven Artificial Intelligence Framework for Analyzing DNA Repair Mechanisms

A biology-driven artificial intelligence framework can transition DNA repair research from traditional pathway-centered descriptions toward context-aware repair-state inference, according to a review published in Experimental & Molecular Medicine. The authors report that DNA repair pathways safeguard genome integrity under normal conditions but frequently suffer dysregulation across human cancers and other diseases. In tumors, DNA repair defects drive ongoing tumor evolution while simultaneously establishing specific therapeutic vulnerabilities. These molecular vulnerabilities present valuable opportunities that clinicians can exploit through targeted chemotherapy regimens, DNA damage-response inhibitors, and cancer immunotherapy.

While conventional pathway-focused studies have successfully elucidated fundamental DNA repair mechanisms, they lack the analytical scale needed to interpret the high-dimensional data produced by modern precision oncology. Current cancer investigations generate vast volumes of genomic, transcriptomic, imaging, structural, and clinical datasets that traditional methods cannot fully interpret. Recent advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning help resolve this analytical bottleneck by offering computational tools capable of measuring repair activity, predicting repair outcomes, and systematically connecting disparate forms of biological evidence.

To structure current analytical tools, the authors organize artificial intelligence applications into a biology-driven three-wave framework. The first wave focuses on mutational footprint-based repair-state inference, the second wave addresses lesion-level repair outcome prediction, and the third wave encompasses multimodal repair-state inference. Together, these methodological waves support systematic biomarker discovery, patient stratification, target prioritization, synthetic lethality discovery, and structure-guided drug discovery. This framework enables researchers to model sequence-context effects on repair outcomes and link cellular mechanisms directly to treatment responses.

The review emphasizes that artificial intelligence analysis must advance from simple predictive correlations toward experimentally supported biological mechanisms. By integrating molecular, transcriptomic, cellular, tissue-level, microenvironmental, structural, and clinical information, machine learning models can infer dynamic repair states in living systems. The graphic abstract highlights this core thesis, demonstrating how context-aware repair-state inference connects multiscale biological observations to functional tumor vulnerabilities. Evaluating the operational strengths, inherent limitations, and appropriate use cases of each computational model remains critical for mechanistic discovery.

Finally, the authors identify key technical challenges that currently restrict the clinical translation of artificial intelligence in DNA repair biology. Major obstacles include limited model transparency, pervasive dataset bias, imperfect labels, algorithmic overfitting, and the absence of standardized clinical validation. Overcoming these limitations requires developing biologically grounded artificial intelligence frameworks that advance mechanistic discovery. Establishing these computational standards will be crucial for translating complex predictive models into reliable clinical therapies that support precision oncology.

Subject of Research: Artificial intelligence frameworks in DNA repair and precision oncology

Article Title: Artificial intelligence in DNA repair: from mechanism to medicine

Article References: Wang, F., Yang, F., Zhang, B., Zhang, J., Hu, J., Tang, J., & Zhang, Y. (2026). Artificial intelligence in DNA repair: from mechanism to medicine. Experimental & Molecular Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1038/s12276-026-01896-9

Keywords: DNA repair, artificial intelligence, machine learning, precision oncology, mutational footprints, synthetic lethality, biomarker discovery, therapy response prediction, structure-guided drug discovery, DNA damage-response inhibitors, genome integrity, lesion-level repair, multimodal data integration, model transparency, clinical translation, context-aware inference, patient stratification
